title: A Two-Stage Screening Method for Solar Site Viability and Inclined-Racking Value Across U.S. Climate Regions
content: Fixed-tilt photovoltaic design often uses inclination near site latitude, but increased incident irradiation alone does not establish an adequate underlying solar resource or project profitability. Using 2018–2023 solar-resource histories for 54 U.S. cities across six climate groups, this study develops a two-gate preliminary screening method. Gate 1 evaluates the six-year mean annual all-sky horizontal resource before any inclined-racking benefit is credited. An initial 1,400 kWh/m²/year reference was tested against the ordered city distribution; a study-specific breakpoint of 1,525 kWh/m²/year falls between Washington, DC (approximately 1,502) and Nashville, Tennessee (approximately 1,548 kWh/m²/year). The breakpoint routes 37 cities to conventional preliminary economic review and 17 to enhanced project-specific diligence, without implying a universal feasibility boundary. Gate 2 evaluates incremental plane-of-array irradiation from south-facing latitude tilt. Independent hourly all-sky transposition yields a mean city-level latitude-tilt gain of 10.06% and a moderate latitude–gain correlation (Pearson r approximately 0.56). Selecting the modeled optimum fixed tilt separately for each year adds a mean 0.90% beyond latitude tilt. A separate clear-sky horizontal screening comparison misclassifies 16 cities (29.6% of the sample) relative to the all-sky Gate 1 screen. The findings support sequential assessment of underlying resource, atmospheric conditions, and mounting benefit; they do not constitute project-specific energy-yield or financial forecasts.
